paragraphs.title: The Joyful City Facing a Day of Turmoil

easy.explanation: The verse asks why the people had gone up to the housetops.
easy.q: Where had the people gone at the beginning of the passage?

easy.explanation: The KJV calls it a city full of stirs, a tumultuous city, and a joyous city.
Elam bears the quiver with chariots and horsemen, and the horsemen set themselves in array.
easy.q: What military forces are mentioned as approaching the city?

answers: The city appears joyful, yet it faces danger and defeat
medium.explanation: Although the city is called joyous, the passage describes trouble, flight, binding, and military attack.
medium.q: What is the main contrast at the beginning of the passage?

answers: The city is experiencing defeat and confusion
medium.explanation: The rulers flee together, while those found in the city are bound.
medium.q: Why are the rulers fleeing and being bound?

answers: The destruction of the city’s defenses
medium.explanation: The phrase appears in the description of a day of trouble and the walls being broken down.
medium.q: What does the phrase “breaking down the walls” describe?

answers: They may not understand the seriousness of the situation
They have already won the battle
They are preparing to leave the land forever
challenge.explanation: Their apparent activity and joy stand in tension with the coming trouble and military threat.
challenge.q: What may be inferred from the people being on the housetops while danger approaches?

answers: From outward joy to confusion, flight, and enemy preparation
From war to a quick victory
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from the city’s appearance to the reality of trouble, fleeing rulers, and organized enemy forces.
challenge.q: How does the situation develop through verses 1–7?

answers: Quivers, chariots, horsemen, shields, and battle array
challenge.explanation: These details portray a prepared military force approaching the city.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that the danger comes from an organized force outside the city?

paragraphs.title: Preparations for the Siege and Forgetting the City’s Creator

answers: The armour of the house of the forest
easy.explanation: The KJV says they looked to the armour of the house of the forest.
easy.q: What did the people inspect on that day?

answers: They poured them outside the city
easy.explanation: The verse says, “ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool.”
easy.q: What did the people do with the waters of the lower pool?

easy.explanation: They broke down houses in order to strengthen the city’s defenses.
easy.q: Why did they break down some of the houses?

medium.explanation: Their actions were practical preparations for defending the city against attack.
medium.q: Why did the people gather water and inspect the walls and armour?

answers: They did not understand the walls
They did not look to the maker and fashioner of the city
They did not gather enough food
medium.explanation: Although they made defensive preparations, they failed to look to God.
medium.q: What was spiritually wrong with the people’s response?

medium.explanation: The ditch was made for the water of the old pool.
medium.q: What does “a ditch between the two walls” refer to?

answers: God’s call to mourning versus the people’s choice of feasting and gladness
A lack of water versus an abundance of water
challenge.explanation: The Lord called for weeping and mourning, but the people chose joy, eating, drinking, and celebration.
challenge.q: What creates the sharp contrast in verses 12–13?

answers: They prepared practically but did not turn to God
challenge.explanation: They inspected armour, gathered water, and fortified the wall, but did not look to the Lord.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the order of the people’s actions?

answers: It is spoken during a time of peace
It excuses feasting instead of mourning and repentance
challenge.explanation: The saying is used to justify eating and drinking rather than responding to God’s warning.
challenge.q: Why is the saying “to morrow we shall die” not presented as a proper response?

easy.explanation: The Lord commanded the prophet to go to Shebna, who was over the house.
easy.q: To whom was the prophet commanded to go?

easy.explanation: Shebna had hewed out a sepulchre for himself in a rock.
easy.q: What had Shebna prepared for himself?

answers: He would be removed from it
easy.explanation: The Lord said He would drive Shebna from his station and pull him down from his state.
easy.q: What would happen to Shebna’s position?

answers: Pride and concern for personal honor
medium.explanation: His self-prepared monument reflects pride and a desire for lasting personal distinction.
medium.q: What does Shebna’s preparation of a grand tomb suggest about him?

answers: Removal from his place and position
medium.explanation: The image represents his being violently removed and sent far from his station.
medium.q: What is signified by Shebna being tossed into a large country?

answers: It confirms his right to the place
It challenges his right to the place and position he claimed
It describes a journey through the wilderness
medium.explanation: The question challenges Shebna’s assumed authority and self-important monument.
medium.q: Why is the question “What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here?” appropriate?

answers: He sought permanence and honor, but would be removed and tossed away
The tomb saved him from exile
The tomb became his new official residence
challenge.explanation: His desire for a lasting memorial contrasts with the violent removal and disgrace decreed against him.
challenge.q: What is the connection between the tomb Shebna made and the punishment he received?

answers: He remains in office and receives greater honor
He prepares a tomb, is tossed away, is sent to a large country, and is removed from office
He flees, returns, and becomes a military commander
challenge.explanation: These events follow the order presented in verses 15–19.
challenge.q: Which sequence correctly describes Shebna’s fate?

answers: His loss of control and removal from his place
challenge.explanation: The image portrays a person violently cast far away from his position and surroundings.
challenge.q: What does the image of a ball being tossed into a large country emphasize?

paragraphs.title: Eliakim’s Appointment and the Fall of the Peg

easy.explanation: The Lord said He would call His servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah.
easy.q: Who was appointed in Shebna’s place?

answers: The key of the house of David
easy.explanation: The Lord said He would lay the key of the house of David upon Eliakim’s shoulder.
easy.q: What was placed upon Eliakim’s shoulder?

answers: As a nail fastened in a sure place
easy.explanation: Eliakim is described as a nail fastened in a sure place.
easy.q: How is Eliakim first compared to a peg?

medium.explanation: The verse explains that he shall open and none shall shut, and shut and none shall open.
medium.q: What does the key of the house of David symbolize?

answers: To the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the house of Judah
medium.explanation: The KJV says he would be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah.
medium.q: To whom would Eliakim become a father?

answers: In a firm and secure position
In a place used only for burial
medium.explanation: The phrase describes a nail fixed firmly and securely.
medium.q: What does “in a sure place” mean in this passage?

answers: Shebna seeks personal honor, while Eliakim becomes a support to Judah
Shebna controls water, while Eliakim controls weapons
Shebna remains in office, while Eliakim is expelled
challenge.explanation: Shebna is condemned for self-centered pride, while Eliakim is entrusted with responsibility for the people.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast between Shebna and Eliakim?

answers: Even something that appears firmly established may be removed, causing what depends on it to fall
Eliakim immediately returns to his former position
challenge.explanation: The final verse says the nail will be removed and the burden hanging upon it will fall.
challenge.q: What does the ending teach about the sure nail?

answers: It shows that many people and responsibilities depend upon his leadership
It proves that Eliakim worked as a metalworker
challenge.explanation: The vessels represent the honor, people, and responsibilities supported by the appointed leader.
challenge.q: How does the image of vessels hanging on the nail clarify Eliakim’s role?
